## Identifying the features (Y)

- **Y1 = bit 4.** In X3-Y1-Z2, every blue input has bit 4 = 0 in both stimuli. Every green input has at least one 1 there. This fits X3 as "neither" or "at least one".
- **Y4 = bit 3.** Bit 3 separates the examples cleanly in X4-Y4-Z1 and in X5-Y4-Z1.
- **Y2 = bit 1.** In X4-Y2-Z1, blue appears exactly when bit 1 is the same in both stimuli.

## Rules and button mappings (X, Z)

Using bit 4 in X1-Y1-Z3, red appears exactly when both bits are 1. So X1 is either "both" (with Z3 true → red) or "not both" (with Z3 true → blue). Fixing that choice fixes everything else that can be fixed:

| | Interpretation A | Interpretation B |
|---|---|---|
| X1 | both | not both |
| X4 | exactly one | same |
| X5 | not both | both |
| Z3 (true / false) | red / blue | blue / red |
| Z1 (true / false) | yellow / blue | blue / yellow |
| X3 | at least one or neither | at least one or neither |
| Z2 | the matching green/blue mapping | the matching green/blue mapping |

Both interpretations fit all six known tasks. Within each, X3 and Z2 are not pinned down by the examples, so there are four fitting assignments in total. Across them, the new task X1-Y2-Z2 gives one of two answers: "both bit-1s are 1 → green, otherwise blue", or the reverse.

## Cross-component pattern

In A, Z1 and Z3 both send "false" to blue. If Z2 does the same, then Z2 true = green, X3 = "at least one", and the new task gives "both 1 → green".

In B, Z1 and Z3 both send "true" to blue. If Z2 does the same, then X3 = "neither", and since X1 is "not both", the new task gives "not both → blue". That is again "both 1 → green".

So the pattern favours "both 1 → green" under either interpretation. The examples alone do not rule out the reverse, so the answer is not fully determined.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: blue, green, red, or yellow. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> red` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is red.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
